[[File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, Hawk.jpg|thumb|right|Hawk, woodblock print]] '''Utagawa Kuniyoshi''' ({{langx|ja|歌川 国芳}}, {{IPA|ja|ɯtaɡawa kɯɲiꜜjoɕi|}}; 1 January 1798<ref>{{Citation|author=Ōkubo, Junichi|date=1994|place=Tokyo, Japan|contribution=Utagawa Kuniyoshi|title=Asashi Nihon rekishi jinbutsu jiten (朝日日本歴史人物事典)|language=ja|publisher=Asahi Shimbun Company|isbn=4023400521|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%AD%8C%E5%B7%9D%E5%9B%BD%E8%8A%B3-34705|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20161005135719/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%AD%8C%E5%B7%9D%E5%9B%BD%E8%8A%B3-34705|archive-date=2016-10-05}}</ref> – 14 April 1861) was one of the last great masters of the Japanese [[ukiyo-e]] style of [[woodblock print]]s and painting.<ref name="nussbaum576">Nussbaum, Louis Frédéric ''et al'' (2005). "Kuniyoshi" in {{Google books|p2QnPijAEmEC|''Japan Encyclopedia,'' p. 576.|page=576}}</ref> He was a member of the Utagawa school.<ref name="nussbaum1018">Nussbaum, "Utagawa-ryū" in {{Google books|p2QnPijAEmEC|p. 1018.|page=1018}}</ref>
The range of Kuniyoshi's subjects included many genres: landscapes, women, [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] actors, cats, and [[:en:mythical animal|mythical animal]]s. He is known for depictions of the battles of legendary [[samurai]] heroes.<ref name="lubow">Lubow, Arthur. [http://nymag.com/arts/art/features/64470/ "Everything But the Robots: A Kuniyoshi Retrospective Reveals the Roots of Manga,"] ''New York Magazine.'' March 7, 2010.</ref> His artwork incorporated aspects of Western representation in [[:en:landscape painting|landscape painting]] and [[:en:caricature|caricature]].<ref name="nussbaum576"/>
==Life== Kuniyoshi was born on 1 January 1798, the son of a silk-dyer, Yanagiya Kichiyemon,<ref name="Robinson 1961, p. 5">Robinson (1961), p. 5</ref> originally named Yoshisaburō. Apparently he assisted his father's business as a pattern designer, and some have suggested that this experience influenced his rich use of color and textile patterns in prints. It is said that Kuniyoshi was impressed, at an early age of seven or eight, by ukiyo-e warrior prints, and by pictures of artisans and commoners (as depicted in craftsmen manuals), and it is possible these influenced his own later prints.[[Image:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, The arhat Handaka.jpg|thumb|left|Painting of the [[:en:Arhat|Arhat]] Handaka ([[:en:British Museum|British Museum]])]]
Yoshisaburō proved his drawing talents at age 12, quickly attracting the attention of the famous ukiyo-e print master [[Utagawa Toyokuni]].<ref name="nussbaum1018"/> He was officially admitted to Toyokuni's studio in 1811, and became one of his chief pupils. He remained an apprentice until 1814, at which time he was given the name "Kuniyoshi" and set out as an independent artist. During this year he produced his first published work, the illustrations for the ''kusazōshi'' ''gōkan'' ''Gobuji Chūshingura'', a parody of the original [[:en:Chūshingura|Chūshingura]] story. Between 1815 and 1817 he created a number of book illustrations for ''[[yomihon]]'', ''[[:en:Kokkeibon|Kokkeibon]]'', ''gōkan'' and ''hanashibon'', and printed his stand-alone full color prints of warriors and [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] actors.
Despite his promising debut, the young Kuniyoshi failed to produce many works between 1818 and 1827, probably due to a lack of commissions from publishers, and the competition of other artists within the Utagawa school (Utagawa-''ryū'').<ref name="nussbaum1018"/> However, during this time he did produce pictures of beautiful women ('[[:en:Bijin-ga|Bijin-ga]]') and experimented with large textile patterns and light-and-shadow effects found in Western art, although his attempts showed more imitation than real understanding of these principles.
His economic situation turned desperate at one point when he was forced to sell used [[tatami]] mats. A chance encounter with his prosperous fellow pupil [[:en:Kunisada|Kunisada]], to whom he felt that he was superior in artistic talent, led him to redouble his efforts (but did not create any lingering ill-feeling between the two, who later collaborated on a number of series).
During the 1820s, Kuniyoshi produced a number of heroic [[triptych]]s that show the first signs of an individual style. In 1827 he received his first major commission for the series, ''One hundred and eight heroes of the popular Suikoden all told'' (''Tsūzoku Suikoden gōketsu hyakuhachinin no hitori''), based on the incredibly popular Chinese tale, the ''[[Shuihu Zhuan]]''. In this series Kuniyoshi illustrated individual heroes on single-sheets, drawing tattoos on his heroes, a novelty which soon influenced [[:en:Edo|Edo]] fashion. The Suikoden series became extremely popular in Edo, and the demand for Kuniyoshi's warrior prints increased, gaining him entrance into the major ukiyo-e and literary circles.
[[File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, Tiger.jpg|thumb|right|Tiger, woodblock print]]
He continued to produce warrior prints, drawing much of his subjects from war tales such as ''Tale of the Heike'' ({{Lang|ja-latn|[[:en:Heike monogatari|Heike monogatari]]}}) and ''The rise and fall of the Minamoto and the Taira'' (''[[:en:Genpei Seisuiki|Genpei Seisuiki]]''). His warrior prints were unique in that they depicted legendary popular figures with an added stress on dreams, ghostly apparitions, omens, and superhuman feats. This subject matter is instilled in his works ''The ghost of [[Taira no Tomomori]] at Daimotsu bay'' (''Taira Tomomori borei no zu'') and the 1839 triptych ''The Gōjō bridge'' (''Gōjō no bashi no zu''), where he manages to invoke an effective sense of action intensity in his depiction of the combat between [[Minamoto no Yoshitsune|Yoshitsune]] and [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]]. These new thematic styles satisfied the public's interest in the ghastly, exciting, and bizarre that was growing during the time.
The [[Tenpō Reforms]] of 1841–1843 aimed to alleviate economic crisis by controlling public displays of luxury and wealth, and the illustration of courtesans and actors in ''ukiyō-e'' was officially banned at that time. This may have had some influence on Kuniyoshi's production of caricature prints or comic pictures (''giga''), which were used to disguise actual actors and courtesans. Many of these symbolically and humorously criticized the shogunate (such as the 1843 design showing [[:en:Minamoto no Yorimitsu|Minamoto no Yorimitsu]] asleep, haunted by the Earth Spider and his demons) and became popular among the politically dissatisfied public. Timothy Clark, curator of Japanese art at the [[:en:British Museum|British Museum]], asserts that the repressive conventions of the day produced unintended consequences. The government-created limitations became a kind of artistic challenge which actually encouraged Kuniyoshi's creative resourcefulness by forcing him to find ways to veil criticism of the shogunate allegorically.<ref>Johnson, Ken. [https://www.nytimes.com/2010/04/16/arts/design/16kuniyoshi.html "Epics and Erotica From a Grandfather of Anime"], ''New York Times.'' April 15, 2010.</ref>
[[File:Utagawa Kuniyoshi Kanama Goro Immakuni.jpg|thumb|left|''Kanama Goro Imakuni'', woodblock print ([[National Museum, Warsaw|National Museum]], Warsaw)]]
During the decade leading up to the reforms, Kuniyoshi also produced landscape prints (''fūkeiga''), which were outside the bounds of censorship and catered to the rising popularity of personal travel in late [[:en:Edo Japan|Edo Japan]]. Notable among these were ''Famous products of the provinces'' (''Sankai meisan zukushi'', c. 1828–30)—where he incorporated Western shading and perspective and pigments—and ''Famous views of the Eastern capital'' in the early 1830s, which was certainly influenced by [[:en:Hokusai|Hokusai]]'s early-1830s ''[[Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji]]'' (''Fugaku sanjūrokkei''). Kuniyoshi also produced during this time works of purely natural subject matter, notably of animals, birds and fish that mimicked traditional Japanese and Chinese painting.
In the late 1840s, Kuniyoshi began again to illustrate actor prints, this time evading censorship (or simply evoking creativity) through childish, cartoon-like portraits of famous kabuki actors, the most notable being "Scribbling on the storehouse wall" (''Nitakaragurakabe no mudagaki''). Here he creatively used elementary, childlike script sloppily written in [[:en:Kana|Kana]] under the actor faces. Reflecting his love for felines, Kuniyoshi also began to use cats in the place of humans in kabuki and satirical prints. He is also known during this time to have experimented with wide composition, magnifying visual elements in the image for a dramatic, exaggerated effect (ex. ''Masakado's daughter the princess Takiyasha, at the old Soma palace''). In 1856 Kuniyoshi suffered from palsy, which caused him much difficulty in moving his limbs. It is said that his works from this point onward were noticeably weaker in the use of line and overall vitality. Before his death in 1861, Kuniyoshi was able to witness the opening of the port city of [[Yokohama]] to foreigners, and in 1860 produced two works depicting Westerners in the city ([[Yokohama-e]], ex. ''View of Honchō'' and ''The pleasure quarters, Yokohama''). He died at the age of 63 in April 1861 in his home in Genyadana.
==Pupils== Kuniyoshi was an excellent teacher and had numerous pupils who continued his branch of the Utagawa school. Among the most notable were [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Yoshitoshi]], [[Yoshitora]], [[Yoshiiku]], [[Yoshikazu]], [[Utagawa Yoshitsuya|Yoshitsuya]], and [[Utagawa Yoshifuji|Yoshifuji]]. Typically his students began an apprenticeship in which they worked primarily on [[:en:musha-e|musha-e]] in a style similar to that of their master. As they became established as independent artists, many went on to develop highly innovative styles of their own. His most important student was [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Yoshitoshi]], who is now regarded as the "last master" of the Japanese woodblock print.
Among those influenced by Kuniyoshi was [[Toyohara Chikanobu]].<ref>"Yōshū Chikanobu [obituary]," ''[[:en:Miyako Shimbun|Miyako Shimbun]]'', No. 8847, October 2, 1912. p. 195.</ref> [[Takashi Murakami]] credits the pioneering influence of Kuniyoshi affecting his work.<ref name="lubow"/>
==Print series== [[File:A cat dressed as a woman tapping the head of an octopus.jpg|thumb|Utagawa Kuniyoshi variation on the theme of ''[[The Mouse Turned into a Maid]]'']] Here is a partial list of his print series, with dates: * ''[[:en:Illustrated Abridged Biography of the Founder|Illustrated Abridged Biography of the Founder]]'' (c. 1831) * ''Famous Views of the Eastern Capital'' (c. 1834) * ''Heroes of Our Country's Suikoden'' (c. 1836) * ''Stories of Wise and Virtuous Women'' (c. 1841-1842) * ''Fifty-Three Parallels for the Tōkaidō'' (1843–1845) (with [[Hiroshige]] and [[Toyokuni III]]) * ''Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety'' (1843–1846) * ''Mirror of the Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety'' (1844–1846) * ''Six Crystal Rivers'' (1847–1848) * ''Fidelity in Revenge'' (c. 1848) * ''Twenty-Four Chinese Paragons of Filial Piety'' (c. 1848) * ''Sixty-Nine Stations along the Kisokaido'' (1852) * ''Portraits of Samurai of True Loyalty'' (1852) * ''[[Twenty-Four Generals of Takeda Shingen|24 Generals of Kai Province]]'' (1853) * Half-length portrait of [[:en:Goshaku Somegoro|Goshaku Somegoro]] * ''[[Takiyasha the Witch and the Skeleton Spectre]]''
See The Kuniyoshi Project<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kuniyoshiproject.com/Main%20-%20Print%20series.htm|title=Kuniyoshi Project}}</ref> for a more extensive list.

===Themes=== Kuniyoshi's work may be parsed thematically, as in this group of images which feature cats. <gallery mode=packed heights=180> File:Cats_forming_the_caracters_for_catfish.jpg|Cats forming the characters for catfish File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, For cats in different poses.jpg|Four cats in different poses illustrating Japanese proverbs File:Cats_suggested_as_the_fifty-three_stations_of_the_Tokaido.jpg|Cats suggested as ''[[The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō]]'' </gallery>
Caricatures were among Kuniyoshi's themes. <gallery> File:Scrbbling on the storehouse wall.jpg|Scribbling on the storehouse wall File:At first glance he looks very fiarce, but he s really a nice person.jpg|At first glance he looks very fierce, but he is actually a kind person </gallery>

[[File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, Hawk.jpg|thumb|right|Hawk, woodblock print]] '''Utagawa Kuniyoshi''' ({{langx|ja|歌川 国芳}}, {{IPA|ja|ɯtaɡawa kɯɲiꜜjoɕi|}}; 1 January 1798<ref>{{Citation|author=Ōkubo, Junichi|date=1994|place=Tokyo, Japan|contribution=Utagawa Kuniyoshi|title=Asashi Nihon rekishi jinbutsu jiten (朝日日本歴史人物事典)|language=ja|publisher=Asahi Shimbun Company|isbn=4023400521|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%AD%8C%E5%B7%9D%E5%9B%BD%E8%8A%B3-34705|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20161005135719/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%AD%8C%E5%B7%9D%E5%9B%BD%E8%8A%B3-34705|archive-date=2016-10-05}}</ref> – 14 April 1861) was one of the last great masters of the Japanese [[ukiyo-e]] style of [[woodblock print]]s and painting.<ref name="nussbaum576">Nussbaum, Louis Frédéric ''et al'' (2005). "Kuniyoshi" in {{Google books|p2QnPijAEmEC|''Japan Encyclopedia,'' p. 576.|page=576}}</ref> He was a member of the Utagawa school.<ref name="nussbaum1018">Nussbaum, "Utagawa-ryū" in {{Google books|p2QnPijAEmEC|p. 1018.|page=1018}}</ref>
The range of Kuniyoshi's subjects included many genres: landscapes, women, [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] actors, cats, and [[:en:mythical animal|mythical animal]]s. He is known for depictions of the battles of legendary [[samurai]] heroes.<ref name="lubow">Lubow, Arthur. [http://nymag.com/arts/art/features/64470/ "Everything But the Robots: A Kuniyoshi Retrospective Reveals the Roots of Manga,"] ''New York Magazine.'' March 7, 2010.</ref> His artwork incorporated aspects of Western representation in [[:en:landscape painting|landscape painting]] and [[:en:caricature|caricature]].<ref name="nussbaum576"/>
==Life== Kuniyoshi was born on 1 January 1798, the son of a silk-dyer, Yanagiya Kichiyemon,<ref name="Robinson 1961, p. 5">Robinson (1961), p. 5</ref> originally named Yoshisaburō. Apparently he assisted his father's business as a pattern designer, and some have suggested that this experience influenced his rich use of color and textile patterns in prints. It is said that Kuniyoshi was impressed, at an early age of seven or eight, by ukiyo-e warrior prints, and by pictures of artisans and commoners (as depicted in craftsmen manuals), and it is possible these influenced his own later prints.[[Image:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, The arhat Handaka.jpg|thumb|left|Painting of the [[:en:Arhat|Arhat]] Handaka ([[:en:British Museum|British Museum]])]]
Yoshisaburō proved his drawing talents at age 12, quickly attracting the attention of the famous ukiyo-e print master [[Utagawa Toyokuni]].<ref name="nussbaum1018"/> He was officially admitted to Toyokuni's studio in 1811, and became one of his chief pupils. He remained an apprentice until 1814, at which time he was given the name "Kuniyoshi" and set out as an independent artist. During this year he produced his first published work, the illustrations for the ''kusazōshi'' ''gōkan'' ''Gobuji Chūshingura'', a parody of the original [[:en:Chūshingura|Chūshingura]] story. Between 1815 and 1817 he created a number of book illustrations for ''[[yomihon]]'', ''[[:en:Kokkeibon|Kokkeibon]]'', ''gōkan'' and ''hanashibon'', and printed his stand-alone full color prints of warriors and [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] actors.
Despite his promising debut, the young Kuniyoshi failed to produce many works between 1818 and 1827, probably due to a lack of commissions from publishers, and the competition of other artists within the Utagawa school (Utagawa-''ryū'').<ref name="nussbaum1018"/> However, during this time he did produce pictures of beautiful women ('[[:en:Bijin-ga|Bijin-ga]]') and experimented with large textile patterns and light-and-shadow effects found in Western art, although his attempts showed more imitation than real understanding of these principles.
His economic situation turned desperate at one point when he was forced to sell used [[tatami]] mats. A chance encounter with his prosperous fellow pupil [[:en:Kunisada|Kunisada]], to whom he felt that he was superior in artistic talent, led him to redouble his efforts (but did not create any lingering ill-feeling between the two, who later collaborated on a number of series).
During the 1820s, Kuniyoshi produced a number of heroic [[triptych]]s that show the first signs of an individual style. In 1827 he received his first major commission for the series, ''One hundred and eight heroes of the popular Suikoden all told'' (''Tsūzoku Suikoden gōketsu hyakuhachinin no hitori''), based on the incredibly popular Chinese tale, the ''[[Shuihu Zhuan]]''. In this series Kuniyoshi illustrated individual heroes on single-sheets, drawing tattoos on his heroes, a novelty which soon influenced [[:en:Edo|Edo]] fashion. The Suikoden series became extremely popular in Edo, and the demand for Kuniyoshi's warrior prints increased, gaining him entrance into the major ukiyo-e and literary circles.
[[File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, Tiger.jpg|thumb|right|Tiger, woodblock print]]
He continued to produce warrior prints, drawing much of his subjects from war tales such as ''Tale of the Heike'' ({{Lang|ja-latn|[[:en:Heike monogatari|Heike monogatari]]}}) and ''The rise and fall of the Minamoto and the Taira'' (''[[:en:Genpei Seisuiki|Genpei Seisuiki]]''). His warrior prints were unique in that they depicted legendary popular figures with an added stress on dreams, ghostly apparitions, omens, and superhuman feats. This subject matter is instilled in his works ''The ghost of [[Taira no Tomomori]] at Daimotsu bay'' (''Taira Tomomori borei no zu'') and the 1839 triptych ''The Gōjō bridge'' (''Gōjō no bashi no zu''), where he manages to invoke an effective sense of action intensity in his depiction of the combat between [[Minamoto no Yoshitsune|Yoshitsune]] and [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]]. These new thematic styles satisfied the public's interest in the ghastly, exciting, and bizarre that was growing during the time.
The [[Tenpō Reforms]] of 1841–1843 aimed to alleviate economic crisis by controlling public displays of luxury and wealth, and the illustration of courtesans and actors in ''ukiyō-e'' was officially banned at that time. This may have had some influence on Kuniyoshi's production of caricature prints or comic pictures (''giga''), which were used to disguise actual actors and courtesans. Many of these symbolically and humorously criticized the shogunate (such as the 1843 design showing [[:en:Minamoto no Yorimitsu|Minamoto no Yorimitsu]] asleep, haunted by the Earth Spider and his demons) and became popular among the politically dissatisfied public. Timothy Clark, curator of Japanese art at the [[:en:British Museum|British Museum]], asserts that the repressive conventions of the day produced unintended consequences. The government-created limitations became a kind of artistic challenge which actually encouraged Kuniyoshi's creative resourcefulness by forcing him to find ways to veil criticism of the shogunate allegorically.<ref>Johnson, Ken. [https://www.nytimes.com/2010/04/16/arts/design/16kuniyoshi.html "Epics and Erotica From a Grandfather of Anime"], ''New York Times.'' April 15, 2010.</ref>
[[File:Utagawa Kuniyoshi Kanama Goro Immakuni.jpg|thumb|left|''Kanama Goro Imakuni'', woodblock print ([[National Museum, Warsaw|National Museum]], Warsaw)]]
During the decade leading up to the reforms, Kuniyoshi also produced landscape prints (''fūkeiga''), which were outside the bounds of censorship and catered to the rising popularity of personal travel in late [[:en:Edo Japan|Edo Japan]]. Notable among these were ''Famous products of the provinces'' (''Sankai meisan zukushi'', c. 1828–30)—where he incorporated Western shading and perspective and pigments—and ''Famous views of the Eastern capital'' in the early 1830s, which was certainly influenced by [[:en:Hokusai|Hokusai]]'s early-1830s ''[[Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji]]'' (''Fugaku sanjūrokkei''). Kuniyoshi also produced during this time works of purely natural subject matter, notably of animals, birds and fish that mimicked traditional Japanese and Chinese painting.
In the late 1840s, Kuniyoshi began again to illustrate actor prints, this time evading censorship (or simply evoking creativity) through childish, cartoon-like portraits of famous kabuki actors, the most notable being "Scribbling on the storehouse wall" (''Nitakaragurakabe no mudagaki''). Here he creatively used elementary, childlike script sloppily written in [[:en:Kana|Kana]] under the actor faces. Reflecting his love for felines, Kuniyoshi also began to use cats in the place of humans in kabuki and satirical prints. He is also known during this time to have experimented with wide composition, magnifying visual elements in the image for a dramatic, exaggerated effect (ex. ''Masakado's daughter the princess Takiyasha, at the old Soma palace''). In 1856 Kuniyoshi suffered from palsy, which caused him much difficulty in moving his limbs. It is said that his works from this point onward were noticeably weaker in the use of line and overall vitality. Before his death in 1861, Kuniyoshi was able to witness the opening of the port city of [[Yokohama]] to foreigners, and in 1860 produced two works depicting Westerners in the city ([[Yokohama-e]], ex. ''View of Honchō'' and ''The pleasure quarters, Yokohama''). He died at the age of 63 in April 1861 in his home in Genyadana.
==Pupils== Kuniyoshi was an excellent teacher and had numerous pupils who continued his branch of the Utagawa school. Among the most notable were [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Yoshitoshi]], [[Yoshitora]], [[Yoshiiku]], [[Yoshikazu]], [[Utagawa Yoshitsuya|Yoshitsuya]], and [[Utagawa Yoshifuji|Yoshifuji]]. Typically his students began an apprenticeship in which they worked primarily on [[:en:musha-e|musha-e]] in a style similar to that of their master. As they became established as independent artists, many went on to develop highly innovative styles of their own. His most important student was [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Yoshitoshi]], who is now regarded as the "last master" of the Japanese woodblock print.
Among those influenced by Kuniyoshi was [[Toyohara Chikanobu]].<ref>"Yōshū Chikanobu [obituary]," ''[[:en:Miyako Shimbun|Miyako Shimbun]]'', No. 8847, October 2, 1912. p. 195.</ref> [[Takashi Murakami]] credits the pioneering influence of Kuniyoshi affecting his work.<ref name="lubow"/>
==Print series== [[File:A cat dressed as a woman tapping the head of an octopus.jpg|thumb|Utagawa Kuniyoshi variation on the theme of ''[[The Mouse Turned into a Maid]]'']] Here is a partial list of his print series, with dates: * ''[[:en:Illustrated Abridged Biography of the Founder|Illustrated Abridged Biography of the Founder]]'' (c. 1831) * ''Famous Views of the Eastern Capital'' (c. 1834) * ''Heroes of Our Country's Suikoden'' (c. 1836) * ''Stories of Wise and Virtuous Women'' (c. 1841-1842) * ''Fifty-Three Parallels for the Tōkaidō'' (1843–1845) (with [[Hiroshige]] and [[Toyokuni III]]) * ''Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety'' (1843–1846) * ''Mirror of the Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety'' (1844–1846) * ''Six Crystal Rivers'' (1847–1848) * ''Fidelity in Revenge'' (c. 1848) * ''Twenty-Four Chinese Paragons of Filial Piety'' (c. 1848) * ''Sixty-Nine Stations along the Kisokaido'' (1852) * ''Portraits of Samurai of True Loyalty'' (1852) * ''[[Twenty-Four Generals of Takeda Shingen|24 Generals of Kai Province]]'' (1853) * Half-length portrait of [[:en:Goshaku Somegoro|Goshaku Somegoro]] * ''[[Takiyasha the Witch and the Skeleton Spectre]]''
See The Kuniyoshi Project<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kuniyoshiproject.com/Main%20-%20Print%20series.htm|title=Kuniyoshi Project}}</ref> for a more extensive list.

===Themes=== Kuniyoshi's work may be parsed thematically, as in this group of images which feature cats. <gallery mode=packed heights=180> File:Cats_forming_the_caracters_for_catfish.jpg|Cats forming the characters for catfish File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, For cats in different poses.jpg|Four cats in different poses illustrating Japanese proverbs File:Cats_suggested_as_the_fifty-three_stations_of_the_Tokaido.jpg|Cats suggested as ''[[The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō]]'' </gallery>
Caricatures were among Kuniyoshi's themes. <gallery> File:Scrbbling on the storehouse wall.jpg|Scribbling on the storehouse wall File:At first glance he looks very fiarce, but he s really a nice person.jpg|At first glance he looks very fierce, but he is actually a kind person </gallery>

[[File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, Hawk.jpg|thumb|right|Hawk, woodblock print]] '''Utagawa Kuniyoshi''' ({{langx|ja|歌川 国芳}}, {{IPA|ja|ɯtaɡawa kɯɲiꜜjoɕi|}}; 1 January 1798<ref>{{Citation|author=Ōkubo, Junichi|date=1994|place=Tokyo, Japan|contribution=Utagawa Kuniyoshi|title=Asashi Nihon rekishi jinbutsu jiten (朝日日本歴史人物事典)|language=ja|publisher=Asahi Shimbun Company|isbn=4023400521|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%AD%8C%E5%B7%9D%E5%9B%BD%E8%8A%B3-34705|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20161005135719/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%AD%8C%E5%B7%9D%E5%9B%BD%E8%8A%B3-34705|archive-date=2016-10-05}}</ref> – 14 April 1861) was one of the last great masters of the Japanese [[ukiyo-e]] style of [[woodblock print]]s and painting.<ref name="nussbaum576">Nussbaum, Louis Frédéric ''et al'' (2005). "Kuniyoshi" in {{Google books|p2QnPijAEmEC|''Japan Encyclopedia,'' p. 576.|page=576}}</ref> He was a member of the Utagawa school.<ref name="nussbaum1018">Nussbaum, "Utagawa-ryū" in {{Google books|p2QnPijAEmEC|p. 1018.|page=1018}}</ref>
The range of Kuniyoshi's subjects included many genres: landscapes, women, [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] actors, cats, and [[:en:mythical animal|mythical animal]]s. He is known for depictions of the battles of legendary [[samurai]] heroes.<ref name="lubow">Lubow, Arthur. [http://nymag.com/arts/art/features/64470/ "Everything But the Robots: A Kuniyoshi Retrospective Reveals the Roots of Manga,"] ''New York Magazine.'' March 7, 2010.</ref> His artwork incorporated aspects of Western representation in [[:en:landscape painting|landscape painting]] and [[:en:caricature|caricature]].<ref name="nussbaum576"/>
==Life== Kuniyoshi was born on 1 January 1798, the son of a silk-dyer, Yanagiya Kichiyemon,<ref name="Robinson 1961, p. 5">Robinson (1961), p. 5</ref> originally named Yoshisaburō. Apparently he assisted his father's business as a pattern designer, and some have suggested that this experience influenced his rich use of color and textile patterns in prints. It is said that Kuniyoshi was impressed, at an early age of seven or eight, by ukiyo-e warrior prints, and by pictures of artisans and commoners (as depicted in craftsmen manuals), and it is possible these influenced his own later prints.[[Image:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, The arhat Handaka.jpg|thumb|left|Painting of the [[:en:Arhat|Arhat]] Handaka ([[:en:British Museum|British Museum]])]]
Yoshisaburō proved his drawing talents at age 12, quickly attracting the attention of the famous ukiyo-e print master [[Utagawa Toyokuni]].<ref name="nussbaum1018"/> He was officially admitted to Toyokuni's studio in 1811, and became one of his chief pupils. He remained an apprentice until 1814, at which time he was given the name "Kuniyoshi" and set out as an independent artist. During this year he produced his first published work, the illustrations for the ''kusazōshi'' ''gōkan'' ''Gobuji Chūshingura'', a parody of the original [[:en:Chūshingura|Chūshingura]] story. Between 1815 and 1817 he created a number of book illustrations for ''[[yomihon]]'', ''[[:en:Kokkeibon|Kokkeibon]]'', ''gōkan'' and ''hanashibon'', and printed his stand-alone full color prints of warriors and [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] actors.
Despite his promising debut, the young Kuniyoshi failed to produce many works between 1818 and 1827, probably due to a lack of commissions from publishers, and the competition of other artists within the Utagawa school (Utagawa-''ryū'').<ref name="nussbaum1018"/> However, during this time he did produce pictures of beautiful women ('[[:en:Bijin-ga|Bijin-ga]]') and experimented with large textile patterns and light-and-shadow effects found in Western art, although his attempts showed more imitation than real understanding of these principles.
His economic situation turned desperate at one point when he was forced to sell used [[tatami]] mats. A chance encounter with his prosperous fellow pupil [[:en:Kunisada|Kunisada]], to whom he felt that he was superior in artistic talent, led him to redouble his efforts (but did not create any lingering ill-feeling between the two, who later collaborated on a number of series).
During the 1820s, Kuniyoshi produced a number of heroic [[triptych]]s that show the first signs of an individual style. In 1827 he received his first major commission for the series, ''One hundred and eight heroes of the popular Suikoden all told'' (''Tsūzoku Suikoden gōketsu hyakuhachinin no hitori''), based on the incredibly popular Chinese tale, the ''[[Shuihu Zhuan]]''. In this series Kuniyoshi illustrated individual heroes on single-sheets, drawing tattoos on his heroes, a novelty which soon influenced [[:en:Edo|Edo]] fashion. The Suikoden series became extremely popular in Edo, and the demand for Kuniyoshi's warrior prints increased, gaining him entrance into the major ukiyo-e and literary circles.
[[File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, Tiger.jpg|thumb|right|Tiger, woodblock print]]
He continued to produce warrior prints, drawing much of his subjects from war tales such as ''Tale of the Heike'' ({{Lang|ja-latn|[[:en:Heike monogatari|Heike monogatari]]}}) and ''The rise and fall of the Minamoto and the Taira'' (''[[:en:Genpei Seisuiki|Genpei Seisuiki]]''). His warrior prints were unique in that they depicted legendary popular figures with an added stress on dreams, ghostly apparitions, omens, and superhuman feats. This subject matter is instilled in his works ''The ghost of [[Taira no Tomomori]] at Daimotsu bay'' (''Taira Tomomori borei no zu'') and the 1839 triptych ''The Gōjō bridge'' (''Gōjō no bashi no zu''), where he manages to invoke an effective sense of action intensity in his depiction of the combat between [[Minamoto no Yoshitsune|Yoshitsune]] and [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]]. These new thematic styles satisfied the public's interest in the ghastly, exciting, and bizarre that was growing during the time.
The [[Tenpō Reforms]] of 1841–1843 aimed to alleviate economic crisis by controlling public displays of luxury and wealth, and the illustration of courtesans and actors in ''ukiyō-e'' was officially banned at that time. This may have had some influence on Kuniyoshi's production of caricature prints or comic pictures (''giga''), which were used to disguise actual actors and courtesans. Many of these symbolically and humorously criticized the shogunate (such as the 1843 design showing [[:en:Minamoto no Yorimitsu|Minamoto no Yorimitsu]] asleep, haunted by the Earth Spider and his demons) and became popular among the politically dissatisfied public. Timothy Clark, curator of Japanese art at the [[:en:British Museum|British Museum]], asserts that the repressive conventions of the day produced unintended consequences. The government-created limitations became a kind of artistic challenge which actually encouraged Kuniyoshi's creative resourcefulness by forcing him to find ways to veil criticism of the shogunate allegorically.<ref>Johnson, Ken. [https://www.nytimes.com/2010/04/16/arts/design/16kuniyoshi.html "Epics and Erotica From a Grandfather of Anime"], ''New York Times.'' April 15, 2010.</ref>
[[File:Utagawa Kuniyoshi Kanama Goro Immakuni.jpg|thumb|left|''Kanama Goro Imakuni'', woodblock print ([[:en:National Museum, Warsaw|National Museum]], Warsaw)]]
During the decade leading up to the reforms, Kuniyoshi also produced landscape prints (''fūkeiga''), which were outside the bounds of censorship and catered to the rising popularity of personal travel in late [[:en:Edo Japan|Edo Japan]]. Notable among these were ''Famous products of the provinces'' (''Sankai meisan zukushi'', c. 1828–30)—where he incorporated Western shading and perspective and pigments—and ''Famous views of the Eastern capital'' in the early 1830s, which was certainly influenced by [[:en:Hokusai|Hokusai]]'s early-1830s ''[[Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji]]'' (''Fugaku sanjūrokkei''). Kuniyoshi also produced during this time works of purely natural subject matter, notably of animals, birds and fish that mimicked traditional Japanese and Chinese painting.
In the late 1840s, Kuniyoshi began again to illustrate actor prints, this time evading censorship (or simply evoking creativity) through childish, cartoon-like portraits of famous kabuki actors, the most notable being "Scribbling on the storehouse wall" (''Nitakaragurakabe no mudagaki''). Here he creatively used elementary, childlike script sloppily written in [[:en:Kana|Kana]] under the actor faces. Reflecting his love for felines, Kuniyoshi also began to use cats in the place of humans in kabuki and satirical prints. He is also known during this time to have experimented with wide composition, magnifying visual elements in the image for a dramatic, exaggerated effect (ex. ''Masakado's daughter the princess Takiyasha, at the old Soma palace''). In 1856 Kuniyoshi suffered from palsy, which caused him much difficulty in moving his limbs. It is said that his works from this point onward were noticeably weaker in the use of line and overall vitality. Before his death in 1861, Kuniyoshi was able to witness the opening of the port city of [[Yokohama]] to foreigners, and in 1860 produced two works depicting Westerners in the city ([[Yokohama-e]], ex. ''View of Honchō'' and ''The pleasure quarters, Yokohama''). He died at the age of 63 in April 1861 in his home in Genyadana.
==Pupils== Kuniyoshi was an excellent teacher and had numerous pupils who continued his branch of the Utagawa school. Among the most notable were [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Yoshitoshi]], [[Yoshitora]], [[Yoshiiku]], [[Yoshikazu]], [[Utagawa Yoshitsuya|Yoshitsuya]], and [[Utagawa Yoshifuji|Yoshifuji]]. Typically his students began an apprenticeship in which they worked primarily on [[:en:musha-e|musha-e]] in a style similar to that of their master. As they became established as independent artists, many went on to develop highly innovative styles of their own. His most important student was [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Yoshitoshi]], who is now regarded as the "last master" of the Japanese woodblock print.
Among those influenced by Kuniyoshi was [[Toyohara Chikanobu]].<ref>"Yōshū Chikanobu [obituary]," ''[[:en:Miyako Shimbun|Miyako Shimbun]]'', No. 8847, October 2, 1912. p. 195.</ref> [[Takashi Murakami]] credits the pioneering influence of Kuniyoshi affecting his work.<ref name="lubow"/>
==Print series== [[File:A cat dressed as a woman tapping the head of an octopus.jpg|thumb|Utagawa Kuniyoshi variation on the theme of ''[[The Mouse Turned into a Maid]]'']] Here is a partial list of his print series, with dates: * ''[[:en:Illustrated Abridged Biography of the Founder|Illustrated Abridged Biography of the Founder]]'' (c. 1831) * ''Famous Views of the Eastern Capital'' (c. 1834) * ''Heroes of Our Country's Suikoden'' (c. 1836) * ''Stories of Wise and Virtuous Women'' (c. 1841-1842) * ''Fifty-Three Parallels for the Tōkaidō'' (1843–1845) (with [[Hiroshige]] and [[Toyokuni III]]) * ''Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety'' (1843–1846) * ''Mirror of the Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety'' (1844–1846) * ''Six Crystal Rivers'' (1847–1848) * ''Fidelity in Revenge'' (c. 1848) * ''Twenty-Four Chinese Paragons of Filial Piety'' (c. 1848) * ''Sixty-Nine Stations along the Kisokaido'' (1852) * ''Portraits of Samurai of True Loyalty'' (1852) * ''[[Twenty-Four Generals of Takeda Shingen|24 Generals of Kai Province]]'' (1853) * Half-length portrait of [[:en:Goshaku Somegoro|Goshaku Somegoro]] * ''[[Takiyasha the Witch and the Skeleton Spectre]]''
See The Kuniyoshi Project<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kuniyoshiproject.com/Main%20-%20Print%20series.htm|title=Kuniyoshi Project}}</ref> for a more extensive list.

===Themes=== Kuniyoshi's work may be parsed thematically, as in this group of images which feature cats. <gallery mode=packed heights=180> File:Cats_forming_the_caracters_for_catfish.jpg|Cats forming the characters for catfish File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, For cats in different poses.jpg|Four cats in different poses illustrating Japanese proverbs File:Cats_suggested_as_the_fifty-three_stations_of_the_Tokaido.jpg|Cats suggested as ''[[The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō]]'' </gallery>
Caricatures were among Kuniyoshi's themes. <gallery> File:Scrbbling on the storehouse wall.jpg|Scribbling on the storehouse wall File:At first glance he looks very fiarce, but he s really a nice person.jpg|At first glance he looks very fierce, but he is actually a kind person </gallery>

[[File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, Hawk.jpg|thumb|right|Hawk, woodblock print]] '''Utagawa Kuniyoshi''' ({{langx|ja|歌川 国芳}}, {{IPA|ja|ɯtaɡawa kɯɲiꜜjoɕi|}}; 1 January 1798<ref>{{Citation|author=Ōkubo, Junichi|date=1994|place=Tokyo, Japan|contribution=Utagawa Kuniyoshi|title=Asashi Nihon rekishi jinbutsu jiten (朝日日本歴史人物事典)|language=ja|publisher=Asahi Shimbun Company|isbn=4023400521|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%AD%8C%E5%B7%9D%E5%9B%BD%E8%8A%B3-34705|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20161005135719/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%AD%8C%E5%B7%9D%E5%9B%BD%E8%8A%B3-34705|archive-date=2016-10-05}}</ref> – 14 April 1861) was one of the last great masters of the Japanese [[ukiyo-e]] style of [[woodblock print]]s and painting.<ref name="nussbaum576">Nussbaum, Louis Frédéric ''et al'' (2005). "Kuniyoshi" in {{Google books|p2QnPijAEmEC|''Japan Encyclopedia,'' p. 576.|page=576}}</ref> He was a member of the Utagawa school.<ref name="nussbaum1018">Nussbaum, "Utagawa-ryū" in {{Google books|p2QnPijAEmEC|p. 1018.|page=1018}}</ref>
The range of Kuniyoshi's subjects included many genres: landscapes, women, [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] actors, cats, and [[:en:mythical animal|mythical animal]]s. He is known for depictions of the battles of legendary [[samurai]] heroes.<ref name="lubow">Lubow, Arthur. [http://nymag.com/arts/art/features/64470/ "Everything But the Robots: A Kuniyoshi Retrospective Reveals the Roots of Manga,"] ''New York Magazine.'' March 7, 2010.</ref> His artwork incorporated aspects of Western representation in [[:en:landscape painting|landscape painting]] and [[:en:caricature|caricature]].<ref name="nussbaum576"/>
==Life== Kuniyoshi was born on 1 January 1798, the son of a silk-dyer, Yanagiya Kichiyemon,<ref name="Robinson 1961, p. 5">Robinson (1961), p. 5</ref> originally named Yoshisaburō. Apparently he assisted his father's business as a pattern designer, and some have suggested that this experience influenced his rich use of color and textile patterns in prints. It is said that Kuniyoshi was impressed, at an early age of seven or eight, by ukiyo-e warrior prints, and by pictures of artisans and commoners (as depicted in craftsmen manuals), and it is possible these influenced his own later prints.[[Image:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, The arhat Handaka.jpg|thumb|left|Painting of the [[:en:Arhat|Arhat]] Handaka ([[:en:British Museum|British Museum]])]]
Yoshisaburō proved his drawing talents at age 12, quickly attracting the attention of the famous ukiyo-e print master [[Utagawa Toyokuni]].<ref name="nussbaum1018"/> He was officially admitted to Toyokuni's studio in 1811, and became one of his chief pupils. He remained an apprentice until 1814, at which time he was given the name "Kuniyoshi" and set out as an independent artist. During this year he produced his first published work, the illustrations for the ''kusazōshi'' ''gōkan'' ''Gobuji Chūshingura'', a parody of the original [[:en:Chūshingura|Chūshingura]] story. Between 1815 and 1817 he created a number of book illustrations for ''[[yomihon]]'', ''[[:en:Kokkeibon|Kokkeibon]]'', ''gōkan'' and ''hanashibon'', and printed his stand-alone full color prints of warriors and [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] actors.
Despite his promising debut, the young Kuniyoshi failed to produce many works between 1818 and 1827, probably due to a lack of commissions from publishers, and the competition of other artists within the Utagawa school (Utagawa-''ryū'').<ref name="nussbaum1018"/> However, during this time he did produce pictures of beautiful women ('[[:en:Bijin-ga|Bijin-ga]]') and experimented with large textile patterns and light-and-shadow effects found in Western art, although his attempts showed more imitation than real understanding of these principles.
His economic situation turned desperate at one point when he was forced to sell used [[tatami]] mats. A chance encounter with his prosperous fellow pupil [[:en:Kunisada|Kunisada]], to whom he felt that he was superior in artistic talent, led him to redouble his efforts (but did not create any lingering ill-feeling between the two, who later collaborated on a number of series).
During the 1820s, Kuniyoshi produced a number of heroic [[triptych]]s that show the first signs of an individual style. In 1827 he received his first major commission for the series, ''One hundred and eight heroes of the popular Suikoden all told'' (''Tsūzoku Suikoden gōketsu hyakuhachinin no hitori''), based on the incredibly popular Chinese tale, the ''[[Shuihu Zhuan]]''. In this series Kuniyoshi illustrated individual heroes on single-sheets, drawing tattoos on his heroes, a novelty which soon influenced [[:en:Edo|Edo]] fashion. The Suikoden series became extremely popular in Edo, and the demand for Kuniyoshi's warrior prints increased, gaining him entrance into the major ukiyo-e and literary circles.
[[File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, Tiger.jpg|thumb|right|Tiger, woodblock print]]
He continued to produce warrior prints, drawing much of his subjects from war tales such as ''Tale of the Heike'' ({{Lang|ja-latn|[[:en:Heike monogatari|Heike monogatari]]}}) and ''The rise and fall of the Minamoto and the Taira'' (''[[:en:Genpei Seisuiki|Genpei Seisuiki]]''). His warrior prints were unique in that they depicted legendary popular figures with an added stress on dreams, ghostly apparitions, omens, and superhuman feats. This subject matter is instilled in his works ''The ghost of [[Taira no Tomomori]] at Daimotsu bay'' (''Taira Tomomori borei no zu'') and the 1839 triptych ''The Gōjō bridge'' (''Gōjō no bashi no zu''), where he manages to invoke an effective sense of action intensity in his depiction of the combat between [[Minamoto no Yoshitsune|Yoshitsune]] and [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]]. These new thematic styles satisfied the public's interest in the ghastly, exciting, and bizarre that was growing during the time.
The [[Tenpō Reforms]] of 1841–1843 aimed to alleviate economic crisis by controlling public displays of luxury and wealth, and the illustration of courtesans and actors in ''ukiyō-e'' was officially banned at that time. This may have had some influence on Kuniyoshi's production of caricature prints or comic pictures (''giga''), which were used to disguise actual actors and courtesans. Many of these symbolically and humorously criticized the shogunate (such as the 1843 design showing [[:en:Minamoto no Yorimitsu|Minamoto no Yorimitsu]] asleep, haunted by the Earth Spider and his demons) and became popular among the politically dissatisfied public. Timothy Clark, curator of Japanese art at the [[:en:British Museum|British Museum]], asserts that the repressive conventions of the day produced unintended consequences. The government-created limitations became a kind of artistic challenge which actually encouraged Kuniyoshi's creative resourcefulness by forcing him to find ways to veil criticism of the shogunate allegorically.<ref>Johnson, Ken. [https://www.nytimes.com/2010/04/16/arts/design/16kuniyoshi.html "Epics and Erotica From a Grandfather of Anime"], ''New York Times.'' April 15, 2010.</ref>
[[File:Utagawa Kuniyoshi Kanama Goro Immakuni.jpg|thumb|left|''Kanama Goro Imakuni'', woodblock print ([[:en:National Museum, Warsaw|National Museum]], Warsaw)]]
During the decade leading up to the reforms, Kuniyoshi also produced landscape prints (''fūkeiga''), which were outside the bounds of censorship and catered to the rising popularity of personal travel in late [[:en:Edo Japan|Edo Japan]]. Notable among these were ''Famous products of the provinces'' (''Sankai meisan zukushi'', c. 1828–30)—where he incorporated Western shading and perspective and pigments—and ''Famous views of the Eastern capital'' in the early 1830s, which was certainly influenced by [[:en:Hokusai|Hokusai]]'s early-1830s ''[[Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji]]'' (''Fugaku sanjūrokkei''). Kuniyoshi also produced during this time works of purely natural subject matter, notably of animals, birds and fish that mimicked traditional Japanese and Chinese painting.
In the late 1840s, Kuniyoshi began again to illustrate actor prints, this time evading censorship (or simply evoking creativity) through childish, cartoon-like portraits of famous kabuki actors, the most notable being "Scribbling on the storehouse wall" (''Nitakaragurakabe no mudagaki''). Here he creatively used elementary, childlike script sloppily written in [[:en:Kana|Kana]] under the actor faces. Reflecting his love for felines, Kuniyoshi also began to use cats in the place of humans in kabuki and satirical prints. He is also known during this time to have experimented with wide composition, magnifying visual elements in the image for a dramatic, exaggerated effect (ex. ''Masakado's daughter the princess Takiyasha, at the old Soma palace''). In 1856 Kuniyoshi suffered from palsy, which caused him much difficulty in moving his limbs. It is said that his works from this point onward were noticeably weaker in the use of line and overall vitality. Before his death in 1861, Kuniyoshi was able to witness the opening of the port city of [[Yokohama]] to foreigners, and in 1860 produced two works depicting Westerners in the city ([[Yokohama-e]], ex. ''View of Honchō'' and ''The pleasure quarters, Yokohama''). He died at the age of 63 in April 1861 in his home in Genyadana.
==Pupils== Kuniyoshi was an excellent teacher and had numerous pupils who continued his branch of the Utagawa school. Among the most notable were [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Yoshitoshi]], [[Yoshitora]], [[Yoshiiku]], [[Yoshikazu]], [[Utagawa Yoshitsuya|Yoshitsuya]], and [[Utagawa Yoshifuji|Yoshifuji]]. Typically his students began an apprenticeship in which they worked primarily on [[:en:musha-e|musha-e]] in a style similar to that of their master. As they became established as independent artists, many went on to develop highly innovative styles of their own. His most important student was [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Yoshitoshi]], who is now regarded as the "last master" of the Japanese woodblock print.
Among those influenced by Kuniyoshi was [[Toyohara Chikanobu]].<ref>"Yōshū Chikanobu [obituary]," ''[[:en:Miyako Shimbun|Miyako Shimbun]]'', No. 8847, October 2, 1912. p. 195.</ref> [[Takashi Murakami]] credits the pioneering influence of Kuniyoshi affecting his work.<ref name="lubow"/>
==Print series== [[File:A cat dressed as a woman tapping the head of an octopus.jpg|thumb|Utagawa Kuniyoshi variation on the theme of ''[[The Mouse Turned into a Maid]]'']] Here is a partial list of his print series, with dates: * ''[[:en:Illustrated Abridged Biography of the Founder|Illustrated Abridged Biography of the Founder]]'' (c. 1831) * ''Famous Views of the Eastern Capital'' (c. 1834) * ''Heroes of Our Country's Suikoden'' (c. 1836) * ''Stories of Wise and Virtuous Women'' (c. 1841-1842) * ''Fifty-Three Parallels for the Tōkaidō'' (1843–1845) (with [[Hiroshige]] and [[Toyokuni III]]) * ''Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety'' (1843–1846) * ''Mirror of the Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety'' (1844–1846) * ''Six Crystal Rivers'' (1847–1848) * ''Fidelity in Revenge'' (c. 1848) * ''Twenty-Four Chinese Paragons of Filial Piety'' (c. 1848) * ''Sixty-Nine Stations along the Kisokaido'' (1852) * ''Portraits of Samurai of True Loyalty'' (1852) * ''[[Twenty-Four Generals of Takeda Shingen|24 Generals of Kai Province]]'' (1853) * Half-length portrait of [[:en:Goshaku Somegoro|Goshaku Somegoro]] * ''[[Takiyasha the Witch and the Skeleton Spectre]]''
See The Kuniyoshi Project<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kuniyoshiproject.com/Main%20-%20Print%20series.htm|title=Kuniyoshi Project}}</ref> for a more extensive list.

===Themes=== Kuniyoshi's work may be parsed thematically, as in this group of images which feature cats. <gallery mode=packed heights=180> File:Cats_forming_the_caracters_for_catfish.jpg|Cats forming the characters for catfish File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, For cats in different poses.jpg|Four cats in different poses illustrating Japanese proverbs File:Cats_suggested_as_the_fifty-three_stations_of_the_Tokaido.jpg|Cats suggested as ''[[The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō]]'' </gallery>
Caricatures were among Kuniyoshi's themes. <gallery> File:Scrbbling on the storehouse wall.jpg|Scribbling on the storehouse wall File:At first glance he looks very fiarce, but he s really a nice person.jpg|At first glance he looks very fierce, but he is actually a kind person </gallery>
''The Monster's Chūshingura (Bakemono Chūshingura)'', ca. 1836, [[Princeton University Art Museum]] <gallery> File:Kuniyoshi, Utagawa, The Monster's Chūshingura (Bakemono Chūshingura), ca. 1836 (a).jpg|Acts 9-11 of the ''[[:en:Kanadehon Chūshingura|Kanadehon Chūshingura]]'' with act nine at top right, act ten at bottom right, act eleven, scene 1, at top left, act eleven, scene 2 at bottom left File:Kuniyoshi, Utagawa, The Monster's Chūshingura (Bakemono Chūshingura), ca. 1836 (b).jpg|Acts 5-8 of the ''Kanadehon Chūshingura'' with act five at top right, act six at bottom right, act seven at top left, act eight at bottom left File:Kuniyoshi, Utagawa, The Monster's Chūshingura (Bakemono Chūshingura), ca. 1836 (c).jpg|Acts 1-4 of the ''Kanadehon Chūshingura'' with act one at top right, act two at bottom right, act three at top left, act four at bottom left </gallery>

[[File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, Hawk.jpg|thumb|right|Hawk, woodblock print]] '''Utagawa Kuniyoshi''' ({{langx|ja|歌川 国芳}}, {{IPA|ja|ɯtaɡawa kɯɲiꜜjoɕi|}}; 1 January 1798<ref>{{Citation|author=Ōkubo, Junichi|date=1994|place=Tokyo, Japan|contribution=Utagawa Kuniyoshi|title=Asashi Nihon rekishi jinbutsu jiten (朝日日本歴史人物事典)|language=ja|publisher=Asahi Shimbun Company|isbn=4023400521|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%AD%8C%E5%B7%9D%E5%9B%BD%E8%8A%B3-34705|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20161005135719/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%AD%8C%E5%B7%9D%E5%9B%BD%E8%8A%B3-34705|archive-date=2016-10-05}}</ref> – 14 April 1861) was one of the last great masters of the Japanese [[ukiyo-e]] style of [[woodblock print]]s and painting.<ref name="nussbaum576">Nussbaum, Louis Frédéric ''et al'' (2005). "Kuniyoshi" in {{Google books|p2QnPijAEmEC|''Japan Encyclopedia,'' p. 576.|page=576}}</ref> He was a member of the Utagawa school.<ref name="nussbaum1018">Nussbaum, "Utagawa-ryū" in {{Google books|p2QnPijAEmEC|p. 1018.|page=1018}}</ref>
The range of Kuniyoshi's subjects included many genres: landscapes, women, [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] actors, cats, and [[:en:mythical animal|mythical animal]]s. He is known for depictions of the battles of legendary [[samurai]] heroes.<ref name="lubow">Lubow, Arthur. [http://nymag.com/arts/art/features/64470/ "Everything But the Robots: A Kuniyoshi Retrospective Reveals the Roots of Manga,"] ''New York Magazine.'' March 7, 2010.</ref> His artwork incorporated aspects of Western representation in [[:en:landscape painting|landscape painting]] and [[:en:caricature|caricature]].<ref name="nussbaum576"/>
==Life== Kuniyoshi was born on 1 January 1798, the son of a silk-dyer, Yanagiya Kichiyemon,<ref name="Robinson 1961, p. 5">Robinson (1961), p. 5</ref> originally named Yoshisaburō. Apparently he assisted his father's business as a pattern designer, and some have suggested that this experience influenced his rich use of color and textile patterns in prints. It is said that Kuniyoshi was impressed, at an early age of seven or eight, by ukiyo-e warrior prints, and by pictures of artisans and commoners (as depicted in craftsmen manuals), and it is possible these influenced his own later prints.[[Image:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, The arhat Handaka.jpg|thumb|left|Painting of the [[:en:Arhat|Arhat]] Handaka ([[:en:British Museum|British Museum]])]]
Yoshisaburō proved his drawing talents at age 12, quickly attracting the attention of the famous ukiyo-e print master [[Utagawa Toyokuni]].<ref name="nussbaum1018"/> He was officially admitted to Toyokuni's studio in 1811, and became one of his chief pupils. He remained an apprentice until 1814, at which time he was given the name "Kuniyoshi" and set out as an independent artist. During this year he produced his first published work, the illustrations for the ''kusazōshi'' ''gōkan'' ''Gobuji Chūshingura'', a parody of the original [[:en:Chūshingura|Chūshingura]] story. Between 1815 and 1817 he created a number of book illustrations for ''[[yomihon]]'', ''[[:en:Kokkeibon|Kokkeibon]]'', ''gōkan'' and ''hanashibon'', and printed his stand-alone full color prints of warriors and [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] actors.
Despite his promising debut, the young Kuniyoshi failed to produce many works between 1818 and 1827, probably due to a lack of commissions from publishers, and the competition of other artists within the Utagawa school (Utagawa-''ryū'').<ref name="nussbaum1018"/> However, during this time he did produce pictures of beautiful women ('[[:en:Bijin-ga|Bijin-ga]]') and experimented with large textile patterns and light-and-shadow effects found in Western art, although his attempts showed more imitation than real understanding of these principles.
His economic situation turned desperate at one point when he was forced to sell used [[tatami]] mats. A chance encounter with his prosperous fellow pupil [[:en:Kunisada|Kunisada]], to whom he felt that he was superior in artistic talent, led him to redouble his efforts (but did not create any lingering ill-feeling between the two, who later collaborated on a number of series).
During the 1820s, Kuniyoshi produced a number of heroic [[triptych]]s that show the first signs of an individual style. In 1827 he received his first major commission for the series, ''One hundred and eight heroes of the popular Suikoden all told'' (''Tsūzoku Suikoden gōketsu hyakuhachinin no hitori''), based on the incredibly popular Chinese tale, the ''[[Shuihu Zhuan]]''. In this series Kuniyoshi illustrated individual heroes on single-sheets, drawing tattoos on his heroes, a novelty which soon influenced [[:en:Edo|Edo]] fashion. The Suikoden series became extremely popular in Edo, and the demand for Kuniyoshi's warrior prints increased, gaining him entrance into the major ukiyo-e and literary circles.
[[File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, Tiger.jpg|thumb|right|Tiger, woodblock print]]
He continued to produce warrior prints, drawing much of his subjects from war tales such as ''Tale of the Heike'' ({{Lang|ja-latn|[[:en:Heike monogatari|Heike monogatari]]}}) and ''The rise and fall of the Minamoto and the Taira'' (''[[:en:Genpei Seisuiki|Genpei Seisuiki]]''). His warrior prints were unique in that they depicted legendary popular figures with an added stress on dreams, ghostly apparitions, omens, and superhuman feats. This subject matter is instilled in his works ''The ghost of [[Taira no Tomomori]] at Daimotsu bay'' (''Taira Tomomori borei no zu'') and the 1839 triptych ''The Gōjō bridge'' (''Gōjō no bashi no zu''), where he manages to invoke an effective sense of action intensity in his depiction of the combat between [[Minamoto no Yoshitsune|Yoshitsune]] and [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]]. These new thematic styles satisfied the public's interest in the ghastly, exciting, and bizarre that was growing during the time.
The [[Tenpō Reforms]] of 1841–1843 aimed to alleviate economic crisis by controlling public displays of luxury and wealth, and the illustration of courtesans and actors in ''ukiyō-e'' was officially banned at that time. This may have had some influence on Kuniyoshi's production of caricature prints or comic pictures (''giga''), which were used to disguise actual actors and courtesans. Many of these symbolically and humorously criticized the shogunate (such as the 1843 design showing [[:en:Minamoto no Yorimitsu|Minamoto no Yorimitsu]] asleep, haunted by the Earth Spider and his demons) and became popular among the politically dissatisfied public. Timothy Clark, curator of Japanese art at the [[:en:British Museum|British Museum]], asserts that the repressive conventions of the day produced unintended consequences. The government-created limitations became a kind of artistic challenge which actually encouraged Kuniyoshi's creative resourcefulness by forcing him to find ways to veil criticism of the shogunate allegorically.<ref>Johnson, Ken. [https://www.nytimes.com/2010/04/16/arts/design/16kuniyoshi.html "Epics and Erotica From a Grandfather of Anime"], ''New York Times.'' April 15, 2010.</ref>
[[File:Utagawa Kuniyoshi Kanama Goro Immakuni.jpg|thumb|left|''Kanama Goro Imakuni'', woodblock print ([[:en:National Museum, Warsaw|National Museum]], Warsaw)]]
During the decade leading up to the reforms, Kuniyoshi also produced landscape prints (''fūkeiga''), which were outside the bounds of censorship and catered to the rising popularity of personal travel in late [[:en:Edo Japan|Edo Japan]]. Notable among these were ''Famous products of the provinces'' (''Sankai meisan zukushi'', c. 1828–30)—where he incorporated Western shading and perspective and pigments—and ''Famous views of the Eastern capital'' in the early 1830s, which was certainly influenced by [[:en:Hokusai|Hokusai]]'s early-1830s ''[[Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji]]'' (''Fugaku sanjūrokkei''). Kuniyoshi also produced during this time works of purely natural subject matter, notably of animals, birds and fish that mimicked traditional Japanese and Chinese painting.
In the late 1840s, Kuniyoshi began again to illustrate actor prints, this time evading censorship (or simply evoking creativity) through childish, cartoon-like portraits of famous kabuki actors, the most notable being "Scribbling on the storehouse wall" (''Nitakaragurakabe no mudagaki''). Here he creatively used elementary, childlike script sloppily written in [[:en:Kana|Kana]] under the actor faces. Reflecting his love for felines, Kuniyoshi also began to use cats in the place of humans in kabuki and satirical prints. He is also known during this time to have experimented with wide composition, magnifying visual elements in the image for a dramatic, exaggerated effect (ex. ''Masakado's daughter the princess Takiyasha, at the old Soma palace''). In 1856 Kuniyoshi suffered from palsy, which caused him much difficulty in moving his limbs. It is said that his works from this point onward were noticeably weaker in the use of line and overall vitality. Before his death in 1861, Kuniyoshi was able to witness the opening of the port city of [[Yokohama]] to foreigners, and in 1860 produced two works depicting Westerners in the city ([[Yokohama-e]], ex. ''View of Honchō'' and ''The pleasure quarters, Yokohama''). He died at the age of 63 in April 1861 in his home in Genyadana.
==Pupils== Kuniyoshi was an excellent teacher and had numerous pupils who continued his branch of the Utagawa school. Among the most notable were [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Yoshitoshi]], [[Yoshitora]], [[Yoshiiku]], [[Yoshikazu]], [[Utagawa Yoshitsuya|Yoshitsuya]], and [[Utagawa Yoshifuji|Yoshifuji]]. Typically his students began an apprenticeship in which they worked primarily on [[:en:musha-e|musha-e]] in a style similar to that of their master. As they became established as independent artists, many went on to develop highly innovative styles of their own. His most important student was [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Yoshitoshi]], who is now regarded as the "last master" of the Japanese woodblock print.
Among those influenced by Kuniyoshi was [[Toyohara Chikanobu]].<ref>"Yōshū Chikanobu [obituary]," ''[[:en:Miyako Shimbun|Miyako Shimbun]]'', No. 8847, October 2, 1912. p. 195.</ref> [[Takashi Murakami]] credits the pioneering influence of Kuniyoshi affecting his work.<ref name="lubow"/>
==Print series== [[File:A cat dressed as a woman tapping the head of an octopus.jpg|thumb|Utagawa Kuniyoshi variation on the theme of ''[[The Mouse Turned into a Maid]]'']] Here is a partial list of his print series, with dates: * ''[[:en:Illustrated Abridged Biography of the Founder|Illustrated Abridged Biography of the Founder]]'' (c. 1831) * ''Famous Views of the Eastern Capital'' (c. 1834) * ''Heroes of Our Country's Suikoden'' (c. 1836) * ''Stories of Wise and Virtuous Women'' (c. 1841-1842) * ''Fifty-Three Parallels for the Tōkaidō'' (1843–1845) (with [[Hiroshige]] and [[Toyokuni III]]) * ''Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety'' (1843–1846) * ''Mirror of the Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety'' (1844–1846) * ''Six Crystal Rivers'' (1847–1848) * ''Fidelity in Revenge'' (c. 1848) * ''Twenty-Four Chinese Paragons of Filial Piety'' (c. 1848) * ''Sixty-Nine Stations along the Kisokaido'' (1852) * ''Portraits of Samurai of True Loyalty'' (1852) * ''[[Twenty-Four Generals of Takeda Shingen|24 Generals of Kai Province]]'' (1853) * Half-length portrait of [[:en:Goshaku Somegoro|Goshaku Somegoro]] * ''[[Takiyasha the Witch and the Skeleton Spectre]]''
See The Kuniyoshi Project<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kuniyoshiproject.com/Main%20-%20Print%20series.htm|title=Kuniyoshi Project}}</ref> for a more extensive list.

===Themes=== Kuniyoshi's work may be parsed thematically, as in this group of images which feature cats. <gallery mode=packed heights=180> File:Cats_forming_the_caracters_for_catfish.jpg|Cats forming the characters for catfish File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, For cats in different poses.jpg|Four cats in different poses illustrating Japanese proverbs File:Cats_suggested_as_the_fifty-three_stations_of_the_Tokaido.jpg|Cats suggested as ''[[The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō]]'' </gallery>
Caricatures were among Kuniyoshi's themes. <gallery> File:Scrbbling on the storehouse wall.jpg|Scribbling on the storehouse wall File:At first glance he looks very fiarce, but he s really a nice person.jpg|At first glance he looks very fierce, but he is actually a kind person </gallery>
''The Monster's Chūshingura (Bakemono Chūshingura)'', ca. 1836, [[:en:Princeton University Art Museum|Princeton University Art Museum]] <gallery> File:Kuniyoshi, Utagawa, The Monster's Chūshingura (Bakemono Chūshingura), ca. 1836 (a).jpg|Acts 9-11 of the ''[[:en:Kanadehon Chūshingura|Kanadehon Chūshingura]]'' with act nine at top right, act ten at bottom right, act eleven, scene 1, at top left, act eleven, scene 2 at bottom left File:Kuniyoshi, Utagawa, The Monster's Chūshingura (Bakemono Chūshingura), ca. 1836 (b).jpg|Acts 5-8 of the ''Kanadehon Chūshingura'' with act five at top right, act six at bottom right, act seven at top left, act eight at bottom left File:Kuniyoshi, Utagawa, The Monster's Chūshingura (Bakemono Chūshingura), ca. 1836 (c).jpg|Acts 1-4 of the ''Kanadehon Chūshingura'' with act one at top right, act two at bottom right, act three at top left, act four at bottom left </gallery>

[[File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, Hawk.jpg|thumb|right|Hawk, woodblock print]] '''Utagawa Kuniyoshi''' ({{langx|ja|歌川 国芳}}, {{IPA|ja|ɯtaɡawa kɯɲiꜜjoɕi|}}; 1 January 1798<ref>{{Citation|author=Ōkubo, Junichi|date=1994|place=Tokyo, Japan|contribution=Utagawa Kuniyoshi|title=Asashi Nihon rekishi jinbutsu jiten (朝日日本歴史人物事典)|language=ja|publisher=Asahi Shimbun Company|isbn=4023400521|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%AD%8C%E5%B7%9D%E5%9B%BD%E8%8A%B3-34705|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20161005135719/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%AD%8C%E5%B7%9D%E5%9B%BD%E8%8A%B3-34705|archive-date=2016-10-05}}</ref> – 14 April 1861) was one of the last great masters of the Japanese [[ukiyo-e]] style of [[woodblock print]]s and painting.<ref name="nussbaum576">Nussbaum, Louis Frédéric ''et al'' (2005). "Kuniyoshi" in {{Google books|p2QnPijAEmEC|''Japan Encyclopedia,'' p. 576.|page=576}}</ref> He was a member of the Utagawa school.<ref name="nussbaum1018">Nussbaum, "Utagawa-ryū" in {{Google books|p2QnPijAEmEC|p. 1018.|page=1018}}</ref>
The range of Kuniyoshi's subjects included many genres: landscapes, women, [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] actors, cats, and [[:en:mythical animal|mythical animal]]s. He is known for depictions of the battles of legendary [[samurai]] heroes.<ref name="lubow">Lubow, Arthur. [http://nymag.com/arts/art/features/64470/ "Everything But the Robots: A Kuniyoshi Retrospective Reveals the Roots of Manga,"] ''New York Magazine.'' March 7, 2010.</ref> His artwork incorporated aspects of Western representation in [[:en:landscape painting|landscape painting]] and [[:en:caricature|caricature]].<ref name="nussbaum576"/>
==Life== Kuniyoshi was born on 1 January 1798, the son of a silk-dyer, Yanagiya Kichiyemon,<ref name="Robinson 1961, p. 5">Robinson (1961), p. 5</ref> originally named Yoshisaburō. Apparently he assisted his father's business as a pattern designer, and some have suggested that this experience influenced his rich use of color and textile patterns in prints. It is said that Kuniyoshi was impressed, at an early age of seven or eight, by ukiyo-e warrior prints, and by pictures of artisans and commoners (as depicted in craftsmen manuals), and it is possible these influenced his own later prints.[[Image:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, The arhat Handaka.jpg|thumb|left|Painting of the [[:en:Arhat|Arhat]] Handaka ([[:en:British Museum|British Museum]])]]
Yoshisaburō proved his drawing talents at age 12, quickly attracting the attention of the famous ukiyo-e print master [[Utagawa Toyokuni]].<ref name="nussbaum1018"/> He was officially admitted to Toyokuni's studio in 1811, and became one of his chief pupils. He remained an apprentice until 1814, at which time he was given the name "Kuniyoshi" and set out as an independent artist. During this year he produced his first published work, the illustrations for the ''kusazōshi'' ''gōkan'' ''Gobuji Chūshingura'', a parody of the original [[:en:Chūshingura|Chūshingura]] story. Between 1815 and 1817 he created a number of book illustrations for ''[[yomihon]]'', ''[[:en:Kokkeibon|Kokkeibon]]'', ''gōkan'' and ''hanashibon'', and printed his stand-alone full color prints of warriors and [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] actors.
Despite his promising debut, the young Kuniyoshi failed to produce many works between 1818 and 1827, probably due to a lack of commissions from publishers, and the competition of other artists within the Utagawa school (Utagawa-''ryū'').<ref name="nussbaum1018"/> However, during this time he did produce pictures of beautiful women ('[[:en:Bijin-ga|Bijin-ga]]') and experimented with large textile patterns and light-and-shadow effects found in Western art, although his attempts showed more imitation than real understanding of these principles.
His economic situation turned desperate at one point when he was forced to sell used [[tatami]] mats. A chance encounter with his prosperous fellow pupil [[:en:Kunisada|Kunisada]], to whom he felt that he was superior in artistic talent, led him to redouble his efforts (but did not create any lingering ill-feeling between the two, who later collaborated on a number of series).
During the 1820s, Kuniyoshi produced a number of heroic [[triptych]]s that show the first signs of an individual style. In 1827 he received his first major commission for the series, ''One hundred and eight heroes of the popular Suikoden all told'' (''Tsūzoku Suikoden gōketsu hyakuhachinin no hitori''), based on the incredibly popular Chinese tale, the ''[[Shuihu Zhuan]]''. In this series Kuniyoshi illustrated individual heroes on single-sheets, drawing tattoos on his heroes, a novelty which soon influenced [[:en:Edo|Edo]] fashion. The Suikoden series became extremely popular in Edo, and the demand for Kuniyoshi's warrior prints increased, gaining him entrance into the major ukiyo-e and literary circles.
[[File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, Tiger.jpg|thumb|right|Tiger, woodblock print]]
He continued to produce warrior prints, drawing much of his subjects from war tales such as ''Tale of the Heike'' ({{Lang|ja-latn|[[:en:Heike monogatari|Heike monogatari]]}}) and ''The rise and fall of the Minamoto and the Taira'' (''[[:en:Genpei Seisuiki|Genpei Seisuiki]]''). His warrior prints were unique in that they depicted legendary popular figures with an added stress on dreams, ghostly apparitions, omens, and superhuman feats. This subject matter is instilled in his works ''The ghost of [[Taira no Tomomori]] at Daimotsu bay'' (''Taira Tomomori borei no zu'') and the 1839 triptych ''The Gōjō bridge'' (''Gōjō no bashi no zu''), where he manages to invoke an effective sense of action intensity in his depiction of the combat between [[Minamoto no Yoshitsune|Yoshitsune]] and [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]]. These new thematic styles satisfied the public's interest in the ghastly, exciting, and bizarre that was growing during the time.
The [[Tenpō Reforms]] of 1841–1843 aimed to alleviate economic crisis by controlling public displays of luxury and wealth, and the illustration of courtesans and actors in ''ukiyō-e'' was officially banned at that time. This may have had some influence on Kuniyoshi's production of caricature prints or comic pictures (''giga''), which were used to disguise actual actors and courtesans. Many of these symbolically and humorously criticized the shogunate (such as the 1843 design showing [[:en:Minamoto no Yorimitsu|Minamoto no Yorimitsu]] asleep, haunted by the Earth Spider and his demons) and became popular among the politically dissatisfied public. Timothy Clark, curator of Japanese art at the [[:en:British Museum|British Museum]], asserts that the repressive conventions of the day produced unintended consequences. The government-created limitations became a kind of artistic challenge which actually encouraged Kuniyoshi's creative resourcefulness by forcing him to find ways to veil criticism of the shogunate allegorically.<ref>Johnson, Ken. [https://www.nytimes.com/2010/04/16/arts/design/16kuniyoshi.html "Epics and Erotica From a Grandfather of Anime"], ''New York Times.'' April 15, 2010.</ref>
[[File:Utagawa Kuniyoshi Kanama Goro Immakuni.jpg|thumb|left|''Kanama Goro Imakuni'', woodblock print ([[:en:National Museum, Warsaw|National Museum]], Warsaw)]]
During the decade leading up to the reforms, Kuniyoshi also produced landscape prints (''fūkeiga''), which were outside the bounds of censorship and catered to the rising popularity of personal travel in late [[:en:Edo Japan|Edo Japan]]. Notable among these were ''Famous products of the provinces'' (''Sankai meisan zukushi'', c. 1828–30)—where he incorporated Western shading and perspective and pigments—and ''Famous views of the Eastern capital'' in the early 1830s, which was certainly influenced by [[:en:Hokusai|Hokusai]]'s early-1830s ''[[Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji]]'' (''Fugaku sanjūrokkei''). Kuniyoshi also produced during this time works of purely natural subject matter, notably of animals, birds and fish that mimicked traditional Japanese and Chinese painting.
In the late 1840s, Kuniyoshi began again to illustrate actor prints, this time evading censorship (or simply evoking creativity) through childish, cartoon-like portraits of famous kabuki actors, the most notable being "Scribbling on the storehouse wall" (''Nitakaragurakabe no mudagaki''). Here he creatively used elementary, childlike script sloppily written in [[:en:Kana|Kana]] under the actor faces. Reflecting his love for felines, Kuniyoshi also began to use cats in the place of humans in kabuki and satirical prints. He is also known during this time to have experimented with wide composition, magnifying visual elements in the image for a dramatic, exaggerated effect (ex. ''Masakado's daughter the princess Takiyasha, at the old Soma palace''). In 1856 Kuniyoshi suffered from palsy, which caused him much difficulty in moving his limbs. It is said that his works from this point onward were noticeably weaker in the use of line and overall vitality. Before his death in 1861, Kuniyoshi was able to witness the opening of the port city of [[Yokohama]] to foreigners, and in 1860 produced two works depicting Westerners in the city ([[Yokohama-e]], ex. ''View of Honchō'' and ''The pleasure quarters, Yokohama''). He died at the age of 63 in April 1861 in his home in Genyadana.
==Pupils== Kuniyoshi was an excellent teacher and had numerous pupils who continued his branch of the Utagawa school. Among the most notable were [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Yoshitoshi]], [[Yoshitora]], [[Yoshiiku]], [[Yoshikazu]], [[Utagawa Yoshitsuya|Yoshitsuya]], and [[Utagawa Yoshifuji|Yoshifuji]]. Typically his students began an apprenticeship in which they worked primarily on [[:en:musha-e|musha-e]] in a style similar to that of their master. As they became established as independent artists, many went on to develop highly innovative styles of their own. His most important student was [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Yoshitoshi]], who is now regarded as the "last master" of the Japanese woodblock print.
Among those influenced by Kuniyoshi was [[Toyohara Chikanobu]].<ref>"Yōshū Chikanobu [obituary]," ''[[:en:Miyako Shimbun|Miyako Shimbun]]'', No. 8847, October 2, 1912. p. 195.</ref> [[Takashi Murakami]] credits the pioneering influence of Kuniyoshi affecting his work.<ref name="lubow"/>
==Print series== [[File:A cat dressed as a woman tapping the head of an octopus.jpg|thumb|Utagawa Kuniyoshi variation on the theme of ''[[The Mouse Turned into a Maid]]'']] Here is a partial list of his print series, with dates: * ''[[:en:Illustrated Abridged Biography of the Founder|Illustrated Abridged Biography of the Founder]]'' (c. 1831) * ''Famous Views of the Eastern Capital'' (c. 1834) * ''Heroes of Our Country's Suikoden'' (c. 1836) * ''Stories of Wise and Virtuous Women'' (c. 1841-1842) * ''Fifty-Three Parallels for the Tōkaidō'' (1843–1845) (with [[Hiroshige]] and [[Toyokuni III]]) * ''Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety'' (1843–1846) * ''Mirror of the Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety'' (1844–1846) * ''Six Crystal Rivers'' (1847–1848) * ''Fidelity in Revenge'' (c. 1848) * ''Twenty-Four Chinese Paragons of Filial Piety'' (c. 1848) * ''Sixty-Nine Stations along the Kisokaido'' (1852) * ''Portraits of Samurai of True Loyalty'' (1852) * ''[[Twenty-Four Generals of Takeda Shingen|24 Generals of Kai Province]]'' (1853) * Half-length portrait of [[:en:Goshaku Somegoro|Goshaku Somegoro]] * ''[[Takiyasha the Witch and the Skeleton Spectre]]''
See The Kuniyoshi Project<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kuniyoshiproject.com/Main%20-%20Print%20series.htm|title=Kuniyoshi Project}}</ref> for a more extensive list.

===Themes=== Kuniyoshi's work may be parsed thematically, as in this group of images which feature cats. <gallery mode=packed heights=180> File:Cats_forming_the_caracters_for_catfish.jpg|Cats forming the characters for catfish File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, For cats in different poses.jpg|Four cats in different poses illustrating Japanese proverbs File:Cats_suggested_as_the_fifty-three_stations_of_the_Tokaido.jpg|Cats suggested as ''[[The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō]]'' </gallery>
Caricatures were among Kuniyoshi's themes. <gallery> File:Scrbbling on the storehouse wall.jpg|Scribbling on the storehouse wall File:At first glance he looks very fiarce, but he s really a nice person.jpg|At first glance he looks very fierce, but he is actually a kind person </gallery>
''The Monster's Chūshingura (Bakemono Chūshingura)'', ca. 1836, [[:en:Princeton University Art Museum|Princeton University Art Museum]] <gallery> File:Kuniyoshi, Utagawa, The Monster's Chūshingura (Bakemono Chūshingura), ca. 1836 (a).jpg|Acts 9-11 of the ''[[:en:Kanadehon Chūshingura|Kanadehon Chūshingura]]'' with act nine at top right, act ten at bottom right, act eleven, scene 1, at top left, act eleven, scene 2 at bottom left File:Kuniyoshi, Utagawa, The Monster's Chūshingura (Bakemono Chūshingura), ca. 1836 (b).jpg|Acts 5-8 of the ''Kanadehon Chūshingura'' with act five at top right, act six at bottom right, act seven at top left, act eight at bottom left File:Kuniyoshi, Utagawa, The Monster's Chūshingura (Bakemono Chūshingura), ca. 1836 (c).jpg|Acts 1-4 of the ''Kanadehon Chūshingura'' with act one at top right, act two at bottom right, act three at top left, act four at bottom left </gallery>
Kuniyoshi's work is held in the permanent collections of many museums worldwide, including the [[:en:Metropolitan Museum of Art|Metropolitan Museum of Art]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=Minakuchi, Ishibe, Kusatsu, Otsu, Kyoto|url=https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/55449|access-date=2021-02-17|website=www.metmuseum.org}}</ref> the Princeton University Art Museum,<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Monster's Chūshingura (Bakemono Chūshingura 化物忠臣蔵) (2015-6735 a-c)|url=https://artmuseum.princeton.edu/collections/objects/110647|access-date=2021-02-17|website=artmuseum.princeton.edu|language=en}}</ref> the [[:en:Nasher Museum of Art|Nasher Museum of Art]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=A Warrior on a White Horse|url=https://nasher.duke.edu/artwork/1374/|access-date=2021-02-17|website=Nasher Museum of Art at Duke University|language=en-US}}</ref> the
